definition: Evasive means avoiding a direct answer or commitment.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word evasive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know evasive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Asked how the driving test had gone, Lena turned evasive and offered a detailed report on the weather instead.
A guarded witness still answers, just carefully and without volunteering extras; an evasive one steers around the question itself.
Stonewalling passes evasive on the same road: the evasive speaker dodges and deflects, while the stonewaller simply refuses to engage at all, question after question.

Cagey means wary and reluctant to give anything away — the caution of someone protecting an advantage, volunteering nothing. Evasive is more active: when a direct question lands, the evasive speaker steers around it. Cagey holds back; evasive dodges.

Noncommittal means refusing to take a side or make a promise — 'we'll see' is the classic noncommittal answer — and it need not hide any facts. Evasive is about the question itself: an evasive reply supplies plenty of words while avoiding the answer that was asked for.

Slippery is the informal word for a person you can never pin down — one who slides out of your grip like wet soap — and it judges the whole character. Evasive describes behavior in the moment: answers that go around a direct question instead of through it.

Evasive is more exact than 'vague' because vagueness can be accidental—a fuzzy memory, a clumsy explanation—while an evasive answer is steered away from the question on purpose.
Evasive describes dodging under questioning—answers that go around instead of through.

A secretive person (another word in this unit) hides things as a standing habit even when no one asks, and to conceal is to hide one particular thing; evasive is what someone becomes the moment a direct question lands and slides off.

My grandmother would answer any question about her crossing except the one I actually asked.
How did you get the exit papers?
She would smile and become evasive, describing the ship's terrible soup, the seasick accordion player, the color of the harbor at dawn.
The details were vivid, generous, and completely beside the point.
My mother warned me to stop expecting more.
The soup got saltier with each telling; the papers never entered the story at all.
Only after her death, sorting through a shoebox of undelivered letters, did I learn what her answers had been built to step around.
